en: Joining with your Alake,
How they slaughtered the Chinese—
My dear mother Kanykei
Had drawn it in a picture:
“Let the orphan see it when he comes;
May their service
Never be forgotten,” she said,
And drew it clearly in a picture.
On this side of it,
Their steeds with piebald heads,
Manas khan's forty nobles—
My dear mother Kanykei
Had drawn them all together.
Then the boy Semetey,
Wailing, weeping, sobbing,
As though they might come back to life,
The boy cried out in tears:
“I never became his guiding mark;
When he wreaked havoc on Kakan,
Joining with my father,
I never became his companion.”
Speaking thus, Semetey,
For the lions gone to the other world,
Recited the Quran for those warriors.
Unable to bear gazing at them,
Urging them on as though alive,
The boy made a lake of his tears.
He went farther on,
To Bek-Jailoo at the head of Besh-Tash;
There is a story to be told.
When Kanykei fled to Bukhara,
With Abyke and the slave Kobosh
Bakai fought fiercely,
Won the name “Bloody Neck,”
Bakai the blood-drinker battled on.
Bakai khan herded camels
In that time of bitter suffering.
For twelve years he fought,
In those days he shot sixty of Abyke's warriors.
Yesterday, when King Manas died,
These were the words of his last wishes:
“When the khan dies, to the old man
His camels will remain close.
Herd the camels, my uncle;
Do not camp at ease.
Now, my uncle Bakai,
Do not live as you did before.
If you go to an assembly, you will see:
If they call you 'White-beard Bakai,'
Uncle Bakai, that day you will die!
Worse than death, my khan uncle,
You will see the face of Judgment Day!
If you disobey, disgrace awaits;
Beginning with this Jelmaian,
Khan uncle, the orphan's camels are entrusted to you!”
The camels Bakai was herding
Had then reached seven hundred.
When he arrived that year,
There were seven hundred camels.
At Jar-Kyia of Jangyryk,
On the path where beasts pass singly,
That the orphan would surely come, hey,
The seven hundred camels knew, hey;
They had filled Jangyryk, hey.
All the camels bellowed, hey,
Bellowing toward Semetey, hey.
They wished to speak, hey, but had no speech;
All together they cried out, hey.
They all ran, ah, swaying,
Their shaggy neck-hair parting, hey,
Their tears spilling, hey.
They surrounded him, hey, and bellowed,
As though gathered at a salt flat, hey,
All sniffing the orphan, hey, and bellowing.
While the camels stood thus, hey,
The prince's heart was torn, hey.
“My father, Prince Manas, hey, do not die!” he said,
The orphan's tears spilling, hey.
“Alas, when even his beasts are like this, hey,
How is my human life worth sparing, hey?!”
Semetey sobbed with the camels;
The prince's son, hey, your dear boy,
Stood wailing then, hey, and crying out:
“To Temir khan's city, hey,
Oh God, I wandered in disgrace;
Hey, my ocean of a father, take me with you!”
Then Semetey, weeping and wailing, hey,
Saying, “Let me die,” hey, yet unable to die,
Unable to take his own life!
Then from those dear quail-like eyes
Tears fell drop by drop, hey.
Those dear currant-like eyes, hey—
The orphan's tears streamed a whip-length down.
The boy wept, hey, and stopped;
The boy's two eyes, hey, had become embers.
Alas, while the orphan stood thus, hey,
Then the camel mother, the gray she-camel in her fifth year,
Came to the boy, hey, bellowing with him.
The camel father, hey, the gray bull,
Came forth with them then, hey, crying out.
Behind those two, hey,
Manas's broad-humped, hey, black hybrid camel,
Jelmaian, left from Manas himself,
Its front lip flapping, hey,
Its rear hump, hey, swaying,
Had a golden halter, hey, on its head,
Counting its years of maturity, ah,
It had fully reached that age.
If you looked at the creature, ah,
It was in its ninety-ninth year, ah.
To my father, Sultan Manas, ah,
It had come from the unseen, ah.
When Manas journeyed to Mecca,
It was found in Lower Medina.
No wind could match its trot, ah;
No beast could match its walk.
Trotting, it skimmed the earth, ah;
All four corners of the round world
It roamed in four days without tiring.
Call it a cloud, ah—it had feet;
Call it an unseen being, ah—it was tethered.
A beast beyond all other beasts was with him;
In battle, ah, it shared his very life.
When he waged holy war on the unbelievers,
When countless troops went to Beijing,
Each day they loaded it with travel rations, ah,
Loaded it with ample ammunition, ah.
When he went to war, it was his merry fellow,
His battle mount, ah, sharing his life:
Zhelmayyan, left by his father Manas.
When dear Manas died,
Poor Zhelmayyan,
Mourning, ah, ate no grass;
Grieving, ah, drank no water.
Mostly among the camels, ah,
It had been wandering, ah.
“When will my orphan come?”
It had no tongue to say the words;
The creature had been grieving.
When it saw Semetey, ah,
Zhelmayyan, sovereign among camels,
Came bellowing and sobbing, ah.
Its white neck wool parted, ah;
Tears poured from its eyes, ah.
On its head was a golden halter, ah,
Good heavens, flashing into sight!
The creature wept like a human, ah;
Then tears poured from its eyes, ah.
“An inheritance left by my father, ah,”
Said Semetey, ah, seeing it,
His heart sorely stricken, ah.
Grieving again, ah, Zhelmayyan
Thrust its head beneath his arm, ah;
Zhelmayyan stood nestled close, ah,
And, rumbling, ah, the orphan
Zhelmayyan kept sniffing, ah.
It snuffled over his hand, ah,
Then sniffed his neck once, ah.
Circling, ah, sobbing,
When he saw Zhelmayyan, ah,
The orphan's soul cried out, ah.
He and Zhelmayyan both wept, ah,
Bellowing and crying aloud, ah.
Now see the wonder, ah:
It circled around the boy;
It turned its neck, ah.
Over a saddle-shaped ridge, ah,
Zhelmayyan went, ah,
Toward Khan Manas's enclosure, ah,
Heading for that enclosure, ah,
Zhelmayyan ran away, ah.
Ah, no beast could match its walk;
Ah, no wind could match its trot.
On Aktulpar beneath him,
Lashing right and left with his whip,
To catch up and seize it—
That was Semetey's thought, ah,
To catch up and head it off.
Keeping beyond Semetey's reach, ah,
Zhelmayyan walked on, ah.
Toward Khan Manas's tomb
Zhelmayyan ran away, ah.
When it reached the white tomb, ah,
It bellowed and bellowed, ah;
Not once, ah, did the creature
Bellow, but three times, ah.
Beside your khan father's enclosure,
Resting on one flank, ah,
Tears welling in its eyes, ah,
Zhelmayyan let them pour.
Now with its head toward Mecca, ah,
Zhelmayyan knelt down, ah.
A golden halter on its head,
Zhelmayyan lay rigid, ah;
Without lifting its head from the ground,
Zhelmayyan lay down, ah.
“My soul, ah, if God Almighty
Would take it,” thought Zhelmayyan, ah,
“If they would dedicate me to the Magnanimous
And sacrifice me,” thought Zhelmayyan, ah,
“If they would cook my sweet flesh
And eat their fill,” thought Zhelmayyan, ah,
“Reciting the Quran for Manas,
If they would slaughter me,” thought Zhelmayyan.
Whipped, it would not rise at all;
Zhelmayyan brought on distress.
For all their efforts it would not get up;
Zhelmayyan caused trouble, ah.
Despairing of Zhelmayyan, ah,
Your orphan dismounted and ran.
To the spring welling up, ah,
Semetey, ah, crying aloud,
Then dipped his hands in the water,
Performed his ablution of the hands,
Now put his feet in the water,
And performed his ablution of the feet.
The Quran's “Say: He is God, One,”
He recited well from memory,
Recited swiftly, without delay.
The saber with its graceful neck
Semetey took up.
“Your soul to God Almighty,
Your merit to my father Manas.”
Praising God's greatness, brave Semen
Singled out Zhelmayyan;
Now your hero sacrificed it,
Now he sacrificed Zhelmayyan,
Now he cut off its head.
On its head was a golden halter.
“My mother spoke of it;
She said it was left by my father, Khan Manas.
Let me take this halter,
Tie it firmly to my saddle straps,
To my valiant, fierce mother
Let me take it as a gift.”
Once he had pulled off the halter,
Once he had tied it to his saddle straps,
Once the halter left its head,
Zhelmayyan vanished into the unseen.
He looked, but could not catch sight of it;
Where it was could not be known.
He looked, but it could not be seen;
No blood had dripped onto the earth,
And Zhelmayyan was gone as well.
There was no sign it had run away,
No tracks where it had walked away.
Thus its desire
Zhelmayyan had attained.
Vanishing from sight,
Zhelmayyan had departed.
For those who truly gave their blessing,
Who had journeyed together with them,
Who had witnessed the holy war,
Zhelmayyan, just as it had been,
On Friday's Night of Power,
On the day of Thursday—
